title: Abiy Ahmed’s Party Sweeps Election, But Tigray Tensions Loom
summary: Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s Prosperity Party has cruised to another parliamentary majority, winning over 90% of seats in this month’s national elections. The Nobel Peace Prize laureate, who took office in 2018 after mass protests ousted the long-ruling EPRDF coalition, campaigned on economic growth and food security in a country scarred by historic famines. Abiy initially won global acclaim for freeing journalists, activists, and political prisoners, and for lifting bans on opposition parties. His 2019 Nobel Prize recognized his peace deal with neighboring Eritrea, ending two decades of hostility. But critics say his government has reversed those gains, detaining journalists and shuttering civil society groups in recent years. Ethiopia has been roiled by violent unrest in ethnically organized regions. In Amhara, the Fano militia has seized swaths of countryside since 2023. A brutal civil war in Tigray from 2020–2022, sparked by a breakdown between Abiy and the Tigrayan leaders who once dominated national politics, killed hundreds of thousands. A 2022 peace agreement ended active combat, but in May, Tigray’s main party moved to reassert control over the region’s administration — a direct violation of the deal. Ethiopian officials and analysts now warn of fresh instability. The electoral board said elections could not be held in Tigray due to “unfavourable conditions.” Abiy’s government projects economic growth above 10% for 2026, among Africa’s fastest. But with the peace deal fraying and armed groups active in multiple regions, the prime minister’s next term may be defined less by Nobel accolades and more by his ability to prevent the country from sliding back into widespread conflict.
why_it_matters: Ethiopia’s stability is critical for the entire Horn of Africa — a region already struggling with climate stress, hunger, and displacement. Renewed civil war would not only cause another humanitarian catastrophe but could also destabilize neighboring countries and create new waves of refugees, affecting global security and migration patterns.

background_read: Ethiopia, Africa’s second-most populous nation, has a long history of centralized rule and ethnic federalism — a system that divides the country into regions based on ethnicity. This has often led to fierce disputes over land and power.

Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in 2018 after years of anti-government protests forced the EPRDF (Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front) to reform. He released political prisoners, lifted bans on opposition groups, and made peace with Eritrea, ending a 20-year stalemate that began with a border war.

The 2020–2022 Tigray war was sparked when Tigray’s leaders, who once dominated Ethiopia’s government, broke with Abiy over delayed elections and loss of influence. The conflict drew in Eritrea and militias, resulting in massive atrocities and a famine-like crisis.

Ethiopia’s economy has been growing rapidly in recent years, but the country remains vulnerable to drought, hunger, and internal violence. Historic famines in the 1970s and 1980s killed over one million people, making food security a constant political issue.

perspectives.description: Abiy’s supporters point to his massive electoral win as proof that most Ethiopians back his vision of economic growth and national unity. The projected double-digit growth offers hope after decades of poverty and famine. They see the Nobel Prize as well-earned and argue that his reforms, including the peace deal with Eritrea, were landmark achievements.

Civil society groups and former allies accuse Abiy of becoming increasingly authoritarian, cracking down on journalists and jailing critics. They see the flawed election — where voting could not even happen in war-torn Tigray — as a sign of a hollow democracy. The ongoing violence shows the government has failed to secure lasting peace or address deep ethnic grievances.

Ethiopia’s ethnic federalism has created a pattern: centralized power struggles often trigger regional rebellions, as historically marginalized groups fight for autonomy. Abiy’s initial promise of reforming this system gave way to a heavy-handed military response, a dynamic seen before in the country. The Nobel Prize underscores how quickly international praise can shift to condemnation when internal divisions boil over.

The 2026 projection of fast economic growth will mean little if the peace deal collapses completely. Key tests ahead include whether the government can hold inclusive talks with Tigrayan and Amhara factions, restore credible elections, and rebuild trust with Western donors who demand human rights improvements. Without genuine power-sharing, Ethiopia risks a cycle of violent reprisals that could unravel the fragile state.
